tagline.text: A turquoise pool and white cascade hidden in a canyon at the bottom of the stairs

location.label: Location
location.text: Outskirts of Iligan City, Lanao del Norte (near the Linamon border)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a day

children.text: True to its name, which means "hidden falls," this waterfall sits hidden at the bottom of a deep canyon, and is the signature falls of Iligan, the city of waterfalls. Descend hundreds of steps and a turquoise pool opens up beneath a white cascade, where you can paddle a bamboo raft right up to the falls and feel the cold spray.

Tinago Falls is set in a mountain valley on the outskirts of Iligan, an industrial city on Mindanao's northern coast, right along the border with Linamon. In Filipino, "tinago" means "hidden," and true to the name, it's completely invisible from the road, revealing itself only after a long descent into a canyon blanketed by dense forest. It's known to stand about
tall, with water fanning out into several strands as it falls down the cliff.

Below the falls is a deep, still pool, its deep water catching the sunlight and glowing turquoise, so it looks like a small lake. The water flows down from the mountain, so it's cold enough to make you shiver even in the height of summer. Beneath the rock behind the falls is a small cave where you can experience up close the space echoing with the roar of falling water, and locals tell a legend of a beautiful girl who turned into the falls and hid in this valley.

Iligan has more than 20 waterfalls in and around the city, earning it the nickname "City of Majestic Waterfalls," and the two most famous are Maria Cristina Falls, beside the hydroelectric plant, and this one, Tinago Falls. Where Maria Cristina Falls is viewed from an overlook after advance registration, Tinago Falls is a hands-on waterfall where you can actually get in the water to swim and raft, making it far more popular with local families and travelers.

Recently the concrete steps and railings have been repaved, and round rest huts and souvenir shops have gone up by the water, making it easier to get around than before. Still, you need to climb hundreds of steps down to the canyon floor and back up, so a basic level of fitness helps. It suits travelers touring northern Mindanao who want a cool natural swimming spot, anyone looking for a day trip from Cagayan de Oro, and photographers who love waterfalls.

blocks.title: The stairway down into the canyon

children.text: About 350 to 500 steps wind their way from the entrance down to the forested canyon floor. The highlight of the walk is the moment the falls start peeking through the trees on the way down.
Grab the rope stretched across the pool and pull a bamboo raft right up to the falls. Getting soaked head to toe in the falling spray is an exhilarating experience.
You can swim in the deep, cold water wearing a life vest. The chill of that first moment jumping in after descending the stairs on a hot day is remarkable.

blocks.title: The small cave behind the falls

children.text: Step into the small cave in the rocks below the falls and the roar of falling water echoes around you. Only enter when the water level is low and staff give permission.

blocks.title: Resting at a hut by the water

children.text: Rent a hut or round rest area beside the pool and relax over a packed lunch. Spending the middle of the day listening to the falls is wonderfully unhurried.
Combine roadside Mimbalut Falls, the cold-spring pools at Timoga, and Maria Cristina Falls, viewed by advance registration, for a full day touring the city of waterfalls.
The canyon is deep enough that light only reaches the pool once the sun is high. When sunlight hits the water in late morning, the turquoise color is at its most vivid.

The final climb near the entrance is narrow and steep, so if driving yourself, take it slowly in a low gear.
Iligan sits on Mindanao's northern coast, so it's rarely hit directly by typhoons, but rain falls fairly evenly year-round with no clearly defined dry season.
February–May
, with relatively little rain, is the best time, with less slippery stairs and a clear turquoise pool. Daytime temperatures in the coastal city run around
, but the canyon floor is much cooler thanks to shade and spray.
June–December

brings frequent afternoon showers, so it's best to visit in the early morning. Right after heavy rain, the falls swell dramatically, but the water turns muddy and the current strong, sometimes suspending rafting and swimming. Weekends and holidays draw plenty of local families, so weekday mornings are quietest. Around the Diyandi Festival, held near the feast day of Iligan's patron saint, St. Michael (
September 29
), the city gets crowded and lodging fills up fast.

There's no lodging around the falls, so staying downtown in Iligan is standard. Business hotels running about
a night and mid-range hotels around

cluster in the city center, near City Hall, the cathedral, and the malls. Cagayan de Oro has far more lodging and dining options and is only about 2 hours away by bus, so many travelers base themselves there and visit as a day trip.

Around the falls entrance are shops selling simple meals, drinks, and snacks, but the menu is limited, so many people buy a packed lunch downtown and eat it at a hut by the water. Iligan is a gateway to the Lanao region, home to many Muslim Maranao, so you can try Maranao dishes served with the spicy condiment palapa, along with dishes like beef rendang. Being a coastal city, grilled fish and kinilaw at restaurants around the market are also cheap and fresh, and about
is enough for a meal.
The stairs are much harder going up than coming down. Allow plenty of time to climb with breaks, and bring enough water.
Wet steps and rocks are slippery, so strapped sandals or aqua shoes are better than flip-flops.
The water is very cold, so bring a towel, spare clothes, and a rash guard, and it's best to keep your phone in a waterproof bag.
The water color is most vivid, and photos come out best, between
10 AM and 1 PM
, when sunlight reaches the canyon floor.
The entrance and the area around the falls take cash only. Bring small bills for the entrance fee, raft fee, and transport.
If you arrive by habal-habal, it's best to arrange a return time with the driver in advance or get their contact number.
To see Maria Cristina Falls as well, apply for a visit with the Iligan City tourism office in advance.
Carry out your trash, and don't use shampoo or soap in the falls' water.
The falls are open daily
6 AM–5 PM

. There are two paths down into the gorge: the Linamon side (about 360 steps, well maintained) and the Buru-un side (more than 500 steps), so if you're worried about your stamina, ask your habal-habal driver to take you to the Linamon entrance.

Iligan is in Lanao del Norte, and the area to the south, Lanao del Sur (Marawi), has often been under travel advisories over security concerns. Before you go, check your home country's regional travel advisory levels for the Philippines, and avoid pushing into mountainous areas beyond the falls and downtown.
The pool is very deep and cold. Even confident swimmers should wear a life vest and swim only where staff designate.
Right below the falls, the current is strong and falling rocks are possible, so it's safer not to swim too close.
After heavy rain, water levels can rise suddenly and rockfalls and mud can spill onto the stairs. Entry may be restricted at these times, so follow local guidance.
The stairs are steep, so those with weak knees, children, and elderly visitors should hold the railing and go slowly.
Entrance fees, operating hours, and raft/swimming rules can change based on the managing body's policy, so check the latest notices.
